title: Second Largest
lesson:
## Lists

Lists store ordered sequences of items and are one of Python's most powerful data structures.

```python
numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, True]
```

### Common operations
```python
lst = [10, 20, 30]
lst.append(40)       # [10, 20, 30, 40]
lst.insert(1, 15)    # [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
lst.remove(20)       # removes first occurrence of 20
popped = lst.pop()   # removes and returns last item
popped = lst.pop(0)  # removes and returns item at index 0
lst.sort()           # sorts in place
lst.reverse()        # reverses in place
```

### Slicing
```python
lst = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lst[1:4]    # [1, 2, 3]
lst[:3]     # [0, 1, 2]
lst[::2]    # [0, 2, 4]  (every other)
lst[::-1]   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]  (reversed)
```

### List comprehensions
```python
squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 6)]  # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
```

### Useful built-ins
```python
len([1, 2, 3])      # 3
sum([1, 2, 3])      # 6
min([3, 1, 2])      # 1
max([3, 1, 2])      # 3
sorted([3, 1, 2])   # [1, 2, 3]  (returns new list)
```
description:
Return the second largest unique value in a list of integers. Assume the list has at least 2 distinct values.

**Example:**
```
second_largest([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]) → 6
second_largest([10, 20]) → 10
second_largest([5, 5, 5, 3]) → 3
```
hint: Convert to a sorted set to get unique values, then take the second-to-last element.
